entry.title: Cape Jervis to Cobbler Hill — Heysen Trail Southern Trailhead Review

link.title: Cape Jervis to Cobbler Hill — Heysen Trail Southern Trailhead Review

entry.content:
The Walk

Cape Jervis is where the Heysen Trail begins — kilometre zero of a 1,200 km marked track that ends at Parachilna Gorge in the Flinders Ranges. There’s something about standing at the southern trailhead with the Backstairs Passage stretching out ahead and Kangaroo Island on the horizon that focuses the mind. Even if you’re only here for a day walk, you’re starting at the beginning of something very large.

The Cape Jervis to Cobbler Hill section runs 14 km through some of the most spectacular — and most remote — coastal terrain on the Fleurieu Peninsula. It tracks southeast from the ferry terminal through exposed clifftop heath above Backstairs Passage, drops to sea level at Blowhole Beach, enters Deep Creek National Park, then makes a sustained final climb to Cobbler Hill at 268 m. Total ascent over the route is 726 m — the coastal undulation adds up despite most of the route appearing flat on a map.

This is a serious walk. The exposure, the lack of water, the clifftop conditions, and the final climb combine to make it genuinely demanding. It’s also, in the right conditions, one of the most beautiful stretches of walking in South Australia.

Cape Jervis and the Opening Stretch

Cape Jervis is a working coastal township — the Kangaroo Island ferry terminal, a general store, a pub and not much else. The Heysen Trail southern trailhead marker is near the foreshore. Fill water bottles here. Genuinely fill them. This is the last point of any certainty before Cobbler Hill.

The opening kilometre or two tracks southeast from the township on a formed foreshore path before picking up the clifftop. The ground rises gradually, the township falls behind, and the Backstairs Passage opens up to the left. From this point the walk earns its scenery rating.

The Coastal Section — Backstairs Passage

This is the centrepiece. For roughly 8 km the trail follows the clifftops above the Backstairs Passage — the narrow strait between the Fleurieu Peninsula and Kangaroo Island. The walking is exposed single track through coastal heath: dense low-growing native vegetation, wind-sculpted shrubs, and the occasional rush of cool onshore air from the Southern Ocean below.

Kangaroo Island sits on the horizon throughout this section, roughly 13 km away across the passage — close enough to see the cliff faces and headlands clearly on a good day. The passage itself is a wildlife corridor: dolphins pass through regularly, and from June to October southern right whales use these waters as they migrate. New Zealand fur seals haul out on rocky platforms at the base of the cliffs below the clifftop trail. Bring binoculars.

The clifftops are fully exposed and the trail demands some care — stay back from unfenced edges, the rock can be crumbly, and in strong onshore winds the section is challenging for the wrong reasons. The best conditions for this walk are a calm, clear morning in the cooler months.

Blowhole Beach

Around the 9.5 km mark the trail descends to near sea level at Blowhole Beach — the lowest point of the walk and one of the more remote beaches on the Fleurieu coast. The descent from the clifftops to the beach level is abrupt and gives the walk a distinct change of character: from open and exposed to sheltered and intimate. This is the natural break point for the walk — roughly two-thirds of the distance, with the biggest terrain challenge (the Cobbler Hill climb) still ahead.

The beach itself is wild. There’s no safe swimming — the Southern Ocean shore break here is powerful — but the setting is remarkable.

Deep Creek National Park and the Cobbler Hill Climb

From Blowhole Beach the trail enters Deep Creek National Park. The vegetation changes immediately: denser native scrub, banksia, and the sheltered character of the park interior after the exposed coastal section. Deep Creek is one of South Australia’s most significant coastal national parks, protecting some of the last intact native bushland on the Fleurieu Peninsula.

The final 2 km is the Cobbler Hill climb — a sustained push from near sea level to 268 m through dense native scrub. The gradient is real. After 12 km of coastal walking the legs will feel it. The trail is well-defined but demands a final effort before the Cobbler Hill car park comes into view.

Highlights

  • Kilometre zero of the Heysen Trail — the beginning of Australia’s longest waymarked walking track
  • Backstairs Passage clifftop views with Kangaroo Island on the horizon throughout the coastal section
  • Dolphins, fur seals and (in season) southern right whales from the clifftops
  • Blowhole Beach — wild, remote, and a natural midpoint break
  • Deep Creek National Park — intact coastal scrub and the most pristine bush on the Fleurieu

Bottom Line

Cape Jervis to Cobbler Hill is the ideal first encounter with the Heysen Trail proper — remote, dramatic, and demanding enough to make you understand why this trail has the reputation it does. The logistics (shuttle, no water, exposed clifftops) require planning, but the reward is a walk that feels genuinely consequential. You start at the edge of the continent and you earn every metre of the climb to Cobbler Hill.

Rating: 4.5 / 5 — One of the best hard day walks on the Fleurieu Peninsula, best in autumn or spring with a calm sea and a clear morning horizon to Kangaroo Island.

Distance, elevation and surface type are derived from a GPS-recorded track. Figures are a close guide rather than survey-grade data — coastal terrain undulation contributes significantly to the cumulative ascent figure. See How Accurate Is Our Trail Data? for detail.

entry.title: Myponga Reservoir Spinebill Loop — Trail Review

link.title: Myponga Reservoir Spinebill Loop — Trail Review

entry.content:
The Walk

The Spinebill Loop is the starter at Myponga Reservoir Reserve — the reserve’s shortest bird-named trail and the natural choice if you’re stopping at Myponga on the way south to the coast, walking with small children or simply want a quick break with a proper water view.

At 700 metres on flat, well-maintained formed gravel trail, it’s a fifteen-minute round trip to the Reservoir Lookout and back. The climbing is almost nonexistent — about 18 metres of gentle undulation — and the surface is reliable underfoot year-round. That simplicity is the point.

What You’ll See

From the Eatts St car park the trail runs gently across the edge of the reserve to the Reservoir Lookout, an open viewpoint across the Myponga Reservoir water storage. The reservoir sits in a horseshoe of rolling hills — farmland and native bush on the higher slopes, the water still and reflective below. On calm mornings the views across the water are quietly beautiful.

The reserve attracts good birdlife precisely because it’s low-traffic. SA Water reserves tend to be undervisited relative to national park walking areas, and Myponga is no exception. Even on the short Spinebill trail it’s worth slowing down at the lookout and watching the margins of the reservoir for water birds.

Practical Notes

Toilets and parking are at the Eatts St car park — use the toilets before setting off, as there are no facilities out on the trail. No dogs are permitted anywhere in the Myponga Reservoir Reserve.

For everything that applies to all the Myponga loops — access, gated opening hours, reserve rules and facilities — see the Myponga Reservoir Walks guide rather than repeating it here.

Highlights

  • Open water views from the Reservoir Lookout over the Myponga Reservoir
  • Flat, accessible formed gravel trail — suitable for any fitness level
  • Quiet reserve setting with good birdwatching near the water
  • Natural starting point for the longer Lapwing and Kestrel loops from the same trailhead

entry.title: Mylor to Cleland — Heysen Trail Adelaide Hills Review

link.title: Mylor to Cleland — Heysen Trail Adelaide Hills Review

entry.content:
The Walk

The Mylor to Cleland section of the Heysen Trail is one of the Adelaide Hills’ most serious single-day walks. Starting from the quiet village of Mylor on the valley floor at 301 metres, the route climbs relentlessly north through conservation land, reservation bushland and the ridge country near Mt Lofty, finishing at Cleland Conservation Park at 616 metres — with a high point of 672 metres in between. Total ascent over the 19.3 km is 925 metres. That’s more vertical than Waterfall Gully to Mt Lofty Summit, spread over more than twice the distance.

This is the section where the Heysen Trail stops being a pleasant walk and starts being a proper long-distance trail. It’s quiet, well-marked with the characteristic white posts and red diamond markers, and passes through genuinely remote conservation land that feels a long way from the suburban Hills towns. Bring it with someone who’ll set a steady pace and not complain about hills.

Setting Off from Mylor

Mylor is a small Hills township about 22 km from the CBD — quiet, residential, with the trail starting at its edge. There’s no dedicated trailhead car park or café; find street parking, fill your water bottles at home, and look for the white Heysen Trail post marking the start.

The first 3 km climbs steadily. Native scrub and eucalyptus close in quickly, and the suburb is behind you within minutes. It’s dense bush with good filtered morning light and, in autumn and winter, the kind of air that makes you glad you started early. The first significant views appear at around 3.3 km on the early ridgeline — south toward Mylor, east over the Hills. This is the first real indication of how far you’re climbing.

The Middle Section — Aldgate and Piccadilly Valley

After the initial ridge the trail moves into more varied terrain around the Aldgate Valley. The route alternates between native bushland and the edges of the settled hills — at one point you’re entirely within conservation land, at another you’re skirting a quiet road or passing through reserve land adjacent to farmland. The vegetation shifts: stringybark and peppermint gum dominate, with native grasses on the drier open slopes.

Around the 7.5 km mark the trail passes through the Piccadilly Valley section — a brief flattening before the main climb resumes. The Piccadilly Valley itself is a significant horticultural area in the Hills (known for cool-climate wine grapes and orchards), though this section of the trail stays mainly within the conservation land on the valley margins. If you’re doing lunch on the walk, this is a reasonable spot for a break — relatively flat, sheltered, and roughly at the halfway mark by time.

The Conservation Park Ascent

From around the 9 km mark, the trail commits to its long sustained climb. The landscape becomes more remote — dense native bush, fewer road crossings, and the elevation gain starts to accumulate seriously. This is Mount George Conservation Park territory, and the contrast with the earlier settled-hills sections is marked. The trail is well-marked throughout but the signage thins to the Heysen Trail posts; there are no interpretive boards or carved feature names.

Over roughly 6 km the route gains nearly 200 metres, reaching 542 m at a high point around the 14.5 km mark. The pace naturally slows. This is where the walk sorts itself out: the reward for the effort is genuine solitude on a well-graded track through intact native vegetation. The birdlife in the conservation park sections is excellent — expect grey fantails, white-throated tree creepers, striated thornbills and, if you’re quiet enough, the occasional glimpse of a Tawny Frogmouth roosting in a fork.

The High Country — Mt Lofty Botanic Gardens Approach

The route hits its high point of 672 metres near the Mt Lofty Botanic Gardens — a managed botanical garden set on the Mt Lofty ranges that is worth visiting separately on another trip. From this elevation on a clear day the views west are excellent: the full Adelaide Plains, Gulf St Vincent, and on very clear days the outline of the Barossa ranges to the north.

The trail stays high across the ridge for a few kilometres before beginning a gentle descent toward the Cleland Conservation Park finish. The vegetation here shifts again — more open mixed scrub characteristic of the upper Lofty ranges, with exposed quartzite outcrops. The descent is gradual and the trail surface is good.

The Finish — Cleland Conservation Park

The trail finishes at Cleland Conservation Park, adjacent to the Cleland Wildlife Park entry on Entrance Road. The wildlife park is worth combining with the walk if you have energy remaining — it’s one of the better places in SA to see koalas, wombats and kangaroos in a managed native setting. There are toilets, a café and car parking immediately at the finish.

If you’ve arranged the Route 823 bus, the stop is a short walk from the wildlife park entry. Check the Adelaide Metro website for current timetable — services to the Hills are less frequent than metropolitan routes.

Highlights

  • 925 m of cumulative ascent through genuine Adelaide Hills bushland — the Heysen Trail at its Hills best
  • Quiet, low-traffic trail with long stretches of undisturbed conservation park
  • Wide ridge views at 672 m toward Adelaide, Gulf St Vincent and the Barossa ranges
  • Excellent birdlife through the conservation park sections — fantails, tree creepers, thornbills
  • Cleland Wildlife Park and Mt Lofty Botanic Gardens at the finish for walkers with remaining energy

Bottom Line

This is the Heysen Trail doing what it’s designed to do — a serious, well-marked, rewarding long-distance section through genuine Hills country. The 925 m of ascent is no joke, and the point-to-point logistics require planning, but the result is a walk that earns its difficulty rating. The conservation park sections in particular feel properly remote despite being less than an hour from Adelaide.

The right audience: experienced day walkers who are comfortable on long hilly routes, prepared for minimal facilities and want something that goes beyond the popular suburban options.

Rating: 4.3 / 5 — One of the most rewarding hard-day walks accessible from Adelaide, held back only by the logistics of a two-car shuttle and the need to carry all your water.

entry.title: Myponga Reservoir Lapwing Loop — Trail Review

link.title: Myponga Reservoir Lapwing Loop — Trail Review

entry.content:
The Walk

The Lapwing Loop is the mid-length option at Myponga Reservoir Reserve and, for most walkers, the most rewarding of the shorter circuits. At 3.9 km with 108 metres of climbing, it threads together the reserve’s most interesting terrain: the forest walk section through denser native bush, the old homestead ruins, and the reservoir outlook — and does it in just over an hour at a comfortable pace.

The character of the Lapwing is different from the flatter Spinebill and Heron loops. Where those circuits mostly follow the formed gravel trail at the edge of the reservoir, the Lapwing pushes into the bushland on the western margin of the reserve, where the vegetation is thicker and the trail has more of the feel of genuine bush walking.

Through the Forest

Starting from the Eatts St car park, the Lapwing climbs gently away from the reservoir through reserve bushland. The gradient is moderate rather than steep — short rises separated by flatter sections — and the surface transitions from the formed gravel path near the car park to the more natural surface of the forest walk section.

The Forest Walk Lookout is reached after the main climb, with elevated views back across the reservoir through the native vegetation. The forest walk section itself is the highlight of the Lapwing — denser, quieter, more characterful than the open sections near the water. This is where the birdwatching is best: honeyeaters working through the flowering understorey, grey fantails following you along the trail, thornbills in the low scrub.

The Homestead Ruins

The Homestead Ruin Lookout is a lookout near the site of farmstead ruins within the reserve — remnants of the farming properties that occupied the Myponga valley before the reservoir was built in the 1960s. SA Water acquired and cleared the land at that time; the ruins are what remains of one of those original homesteads. It’s worth taking a moment here — the outlook across the southern section of the reservoir is good, and the contrast between the managed reserve of today and the farming past gives the landscape an additional layer of interest.

Reservoir Outlook and Return

From the homestead ruins the trail descends gently back toward the water, passing the Reservoir Lookout for an open view across the reservoir before returning to the Eatts St car park. This final section is the same trail used by the Spinebill Loop in reverse.

Practical Notes

Toilets are at the Eatts St car park at the start; carry all water, as there are nothing on the trail itself. Dogs are not permitted in the reserve. Check gate times with SA Water before visiting — the reserve has seasonal gated hours.

For access, opening hours, facilities and the full rules that apply to every Myponga loop, see the Myponga Reservoir Walks guide.

Highlights

  • Forest walk section with the reserve’s densest native bush and best birdwatching
  • Homestead Ruin Lookout combining reservoir views and valley history
  • Relaxed moderate circuit covering the reserve’s most interesting terrain in just over an hour
  • Quiet, low-traffic SA Water reserve — genuinely peaceful mid-week

entry.title: Myponga Reservoir Kestrel Loop — Trail Review

link.title: Myponga Reservoir Kestrel Loop — Trail Review

entry.content:
The Walk

The Kestrel Loop is the full circuit at Myponga Reservoir Reserve — 6.77 km of formed gravel and bushland trail that links every major lookout and feature in the reserve in a single two-hour walk. If you’re visiting Myponga for the first time and have the time, this is the walk to do.

Named for the common kestrel that hunts the open reserve margins, the Kestrel absorbs all three of the shorter bird-named loops: everything in the Spinebill, Heron and Lapwing circuits is included within it. That means the Deck Lookout, the forest walk section, the old homestead ruins, the western reserve and the Reservoir Lookout — all in one circuit from the Hansen St trailhead.

The Opening Section — Hansen St to the Deck Lookout

The Kestrel begins at the Hansen St car park on the northern side of the reserve, passing quickly to the Deck Lookout — a timber viewing platform with a direct outlook over the Myponga Reservoir. On calm mornings (particularly in autumn and winter) the water is still enough to reflect the surrounding hills in near-perfect mirror. This is the reserve’s most photogenic spot and the best point for watching water birds: herons, cormorants and various ducks work the shallow margins below the deck.

Eatts St and the Forest Walk

From the deck the circuit moves to the Eatts St car park area — roughly the halfway point — where the reserve’s eastern toilet facilities are located. Beyond here the trail enters the forest walk section, the denser native bush on the western margin of the reserve. The vegetation closes in, the formed gravel gives way to a more natural bush surface, and the character of the walk changes.

This is the Kestrel’s most atmospheric section: filtered light through eucalyptus and wattle, the quiet of a reserve that sees relatively few visitors. The birdwatching through the forest walk is consistently good — honeyeaters, grey fantails, thornbills and, in the mornings, a noisy and varied understorey chorus.

The Western Section — Ruins and Ridge

Continuing through the forest section the trail reaches the Forest Walk Lookout, elevated above the reservoir with views through the native vegetation, then descends slightly to the Homestead Ruin Lookout. The ruins here are remnants of farming properties that occupied the Myponga valley before SA Water developed the reservoir in the 1960s. The lookout has good views south across the reservoir and the contrast between the modern managed reserve and this agricultural past is striking.

Beyond the ruins the circuit passes through the western section of the reserve, passing the western toilet block before looping back north and east toward the reservoir lookouts.

Reservoir Lookout and Return

The Reservoir Lookout provides an open view across the full width of the reservoir — a different perspective to the deck, with the valley visible in both directions and the reserve’s hills framing the water. From here the trail returns along the southern edge of the reserve to the Hansen St car park.

Practical Notes

Plan around the gate times — the Kestrel’s two-hour duration leaves less buffer than the shorter loops if you arrive late. Carry water (the trail has no water sources) and use the toilets at Eatts St or the western car park midway. Dogs are not permitted in the reserve.

For access, opening hours, facilities and the full rules that apply to every Myponga loop, see the Myponga Reservoir Walks guide.

Highlights

  • The Deck Lookout — reservoir reflections and water birds in the morning
  • Forest walk section: the reserve’s densest native bush with excellent birdwatching
  • Homestead Ruin Lookout: history and elevated reservoir views
  • A complete picture of the reserve in a single two-hour circuit
  • Quiet, low-traffic environment — a proper escape close enough to Adelaide for a day trip

Rating: 4.3 / 5 — The most complete walking experience at Myponga Reservoir Reserve, best enjoyed on a still autumn or winter morning when the light is good and the reserve is at its quietest.

entry.title: Myponga Reservoir Heron Loop — Trail Review

link.title: Myponga Reservoir Heron Loop — Trail Review

entry.content:
The Walk

The Heron Loop is the easy short circuit at Myponga Reservoir Reserve — a relaxed 1.9 km that takes in two of the reserve’s best reservoir viewpoints. Named for the herons that work the reservoir margins in the quieter morning hours, it’s a step up from the flat Spinebill but still accessible to any level of fitness. Allow half an hour at a comfortable pace, more if you stop at the lookouts.

What You’ll See

From the Hansen St car park the trail winds through reserve bushland — formed gravel, gentle grades, no challenging terrain — to the Deck Lookout. This is a timber viewing platform built at the edge of the reserve with a direct outlook over the Myponga Reservoir. On still mornings the water mirrors the surrounding hills; in the afternoon it picks up wind riffles. Either way it’s a genuinely attractive view, and this is the best point in the reserve to look for herons and other water birds in the margins below the deck.

The trail continues past the deck to the Reservoir Lookout, a more open viewpoint that takes in a wider sweep of the water and the valley. From here the circuit passes through the Eatts St car park area — where the reserve’s public toilets are located — before returning along the southern edge of the reserve to the Hansen St starting point.

Birdwatching Notes

The Heron name isn’t accidental. The SA Water reserve environment — low foot traffic, undisturbed water, native vegetation on the margins — makes this a better birdwatching destination than more popular trail areas. Beyond herons, you can expect ducks, cormorants and various small bush birds in the surrounding vegetation. Morning visits produce the most activity; the reserve is at its quietest in the hour after gates open.

Practical Notes

Toilets are at the Eatts St car park — roughly at the midpoint of the loop — not at the Hansen St start. Carry water, as there’s nothing on the trail. Dogs are not permitted anywhere in the reserve.

For access, opening hours, facilities and the full rules that apply to every Myponga loop, see the Myponga Reservoir Walks guide.

Highlights

  • Timber Deck Lookout with direct views across the reservoir — the best heron-watching spot in the reserve
  • Two reservoir viewpoints in under 2 km of easy, well-graded walking
  • Quiet, low-traffic reserve setting ideal for birdwatching
  • Connects directly to the Kestrel Loop from the same Hansen St trailhead

entry.title: Tapanappa to Balquhidder — Heysen Trail South Coast Wilderness Review

link.title: Tapanappa to Balquhidder — Heysen Trail South Coast Wilderness Review

entry.content:
Overview

The Tapanappa to Balquhidder section of the Heysen Trail South Coast is, in a word, wild. It covers 14.75 km of some of the most remote and spectacular coastal terrain in South Australia — clifftop single track, a kilometre-and-a-half of deserted wilderness beach and serious headland scrambles — with 599 m of ascent packed into a walk that demands respect and preparation.

This section sits between Delamere and Balquhidder on the 73 km Heysen Trail South Coast route — a multi-day track running from Cape Jervis to Victor Harbor. As a standalone day walk, it’s classified Hard — not because the terrain is technically extreme, but because of the commitment level involved: remote location, no water, no phone coverage, tide-dependent beach crossing and genuinely dangerous cliff edges.

Get it right and it’s one of the finest day walks in South Australia.

This is a Remote and Committing Walk

No roads access the route between Tapanappa and Balquhidder. No phone coverage for most of the section. No water on route. The tidal beach section can close at high tide. Share your trip plan with someone before departing, carry a PLB or satellite communicator, and do not attempt this walk in poor weather.

The Route in Detail

Tapanappa Lookout to Boat Harbour (km 0 – 2.5)

The walk begins at Tapanappa Lookout — a broad clifftop viewpoint above 200 m that on a clear morning delivers views west toward Cape Jervis (and the lighthouse there), east along the wild southern Fleurieu coast and south to the endless Southern Ocean. Start early to catch it in morning light.

The trail drops immediately eastward from the lookout on narrow single track along the cliff edge. This is technically straightforward but psychologically intense: the track sits close to unfenced drops of 50–100 m onto coastal rocks below. Stay well back from the edge and keep dogs leashed if you have them (though the Conservation Park sections don’t permit dogs).

Boat Harbour appears around km 2.5 — a small, rocky cove carved into the base of the cliffs. The cove can be reached from the trail with care, though access to the water is difficult. More valuably, it’s one of the most reliable dolphin viewing spots on the Fleurieu coast.

Boat Harbour — Dolphin and Seal Viewing

Bottlenose dolphins regularly work the kelp beds in and around Boat Harbour, visible from the cliff track above. New Zealand fur seals haul out on the rocky outcrops at the base of the cove. Between June and October, southern right whales migrate along this stretch of coast — the clifftop vantage is exceptional.

The Descent to Tunkalilla Beach (km 2.5 – 5.5)

After Boat Harbour the trail climbs briefly before beginning the long descent toward Tunkalilla Beach. This is the most technically demanding descent of the walk — steep, rocky, loose in sections and unforgiving if the ground is wet.

The descent takes approximately 45 minutes for most walkers. Trekking poles are very useful here. The trail drops from around 200 m at the clifftop to beach level at Tunkalilla — more than 190 m of descent in under 3 km.

Tide Check — Before Reaching Tunkalilla

Check the Bureau of Meteorology Victor Harbor tide chart before setting out. Aim to arrive at Tunkalilla Beach within 2 hours either side of low tide. At high tide, waves can close off the beach entirely by running directly to the cliff base — leaving no passable route and no safe retreat. This is not an exaggeration.

Tunkalilla Beach (km 5.5 – 7)

Tunkalilla Beach is one of the most remote and beautiful beaches in South Australia. Dark sand, sheer cliffs on both sides, wave-scoured rock platforms and the constant thunder of Southern Ocean swell — and, in all likelihood, not another person in sight.

There is no infrastructure, no safe swimming and no shelter. The 1.5 km beach crossing is straightforward in normal conditions: walk south along the sand until the cliffs converge, then pick up the track ascending the eastern headland.

Whale Watching from Tunkalilla

Between June and October, Tunkalilla Beach offers some of the most raw, unmediated whale watching in the state. Southern right whales pass close inshore along this stretch, and with no infrastructure, no crowds and 200 m cliffs behind you, it's an experience that's hard to overstate. Even outside whale season, orca are occasionally sighted offshore.

Eastern Headland Scramble (km 7 – 9.5)

The eastern headland scramble is the crux of the walk. The trail climbs steeply from beach level over the headland — with sections of rock scrambling where trekking poles need to be collapsed and hands used for balance. It’s not technically climbing, but it’s the most demanding single section.

Allow more time than you think. The views from the top of the headland back toward Tunkalilla Beach — and west toward Tapanappa — are the best on the walk.

Coastal Heath to Balquhidder (km 9.5 – 14.75)

From the headland, the trail rolls through coastal heath and open clifftop country heading east toward Balquhidder. The terrain eases considerably after the headland scramble — this final section is the most enjoyable and relaxed part of the walk.

The trail emerges at Balquhidder campsite — a designated Heysen Trail camp with a basic shelter, a composting toilet and a water tank (do not rely on the tank being filled — verify in advance with the Heysen Trail Association).

Getting There and Away

Start: Tapanappa Lookout, accessible via Delamere Road from the Fleurieu Peninsula. The road to Tapanappa is unsealed for the final section — accessible in a normal vehicle in dry conditions, but 4WD advisable after heavy rain.

Finish: Balquhidder campsite. By road, Balquhidder is approximately 1.5 hours from Tapanappa via Delamere, Yankalilla and Carrickalinga. Plan your shuttle carefully before setting out.

Who Is This Walk For?

Experienced walkers who are:

  • Fit enough for 15 km with 600 m ascent in remote terrain
  • Comfortable with tide-dependent planning
  • Equipped with navigation tools and a PLB or satellite device
  • Willing to accept the commitment level involved

This is not a walk for the unprepared. For fit, experienced walkers who embrace remote coastal adventure, it’s exceptional.
entry.summary: Tapanappa to Balquhidder walk: a hard 14.75 km Heysen Trail point-to-point on the wild Fleurieu coast, SA. Tunkalilla Beach, map & free GPX.

entry.title: Happy Valley Reservoir Boundary Loop — Trail Review

link.title: Happy Valley Reservoir Boundary Loop — Trail Review

entry.content:
The Walk

The Boundary Loop is the full perimeter circuit of Happy Valley Reservoir. At 10.16 km with 173 m of total ascent, it is the most demanding walk in the reserve and the only one that circumnavigates the entire water body. Walking SA rates it Grade 4 Challenging, citing very steep hills throughout — and unlike the Grade 4 Shoreline Loop which is undulating, the Boundary Loop’s climbs are sharper and more concentrated.

This is the walk for people who’ve already done the Shoreline Loop and want to see the rest of the reservoir. It takes a substantially different route, following the outer boundary of the reserve rather than tracing the water’s edge. This means more climbing, more exposure on the western ridge, and — on a clear day — better views across to the outer suburbs and hills.

The trail is also open to mountain bikes and is regularly used by trail runners, making it the most active-use circuit in the network. Weekday mornings are quieter; weekend mornings can be busy near the carpark end.

The Terrain

The elevation range of 148 m to 201 m sounds modest, but the route achieves it via multiple sharp ascents rather than a gradual rise. The western boundary section involves sustained steep climbing and is the point where most walkers will feel the grade most acutely. Good trail shoes with grip are appropriate; poles are useful for the steeper descents.

The surface is consistent with the rest of the Happy Valley network — formed gravel and compacted dirt throughout. There are no technical sections, but the steep grade on loose gravel demands sure footing.

Glenthorne National Park

A pedestrian crossing at the South Road / Black Road intersection connects the Boundary Loop directly to Glenthorne National Park. Glenthorne is a developing national park on the southern fringe of the metropolitan area — trail infrastructure is being expanded progressively. The connection point means a longer day walk combining both reserves is feasible, though you’ll need to research current Glenthorne trail conditions separately as they are not covered here.

Access Points

The main trailhead at the Chandlers Hill Road / Kenihans Road roundabout is the standard start point. A secondary carpark near the dam wall provides alternative access from Manning Road, which is useful for accessing the Minkarra Park section or if the main carpark is full on busy mornings.

Practical Notes

  • Allow 3 hours at a steady walking pace — more if you add Glenthorne
  • Very steep hills on the western boundary — trekking poles recommended
  • Carry 1.5–2 litres of water; no fountains on course beyond the trailhead
  • Mountain bikes and trail runners share the trail — stay aware
  • Reserve closes on Total Fire Ban days — check cfs.sa.gov.au
  • Gates locked at closing time — 5:00 pm in winter; don’t start after 2:00 pm
  • No dogs anywhere in the reserve
  • Green trail markers throughout — follow carefully at junctions near the trailhead
entry.summary: Happy Valley Reservoir Boundary Loop: the full 10.16 km hard perimeter circuit ~20 km south of Adelaide, SA. Steep hills, map & free GPX.

entry.title: Happy Valley Reservoir Southern Loop — Trail Review

link.title: Happy Valley Reservoir Southern Loop — Trail Review

entry.content:
The Walk

The Southern Loop is the entry point to the Happy Valley Reservoir trail network. At 2.39 km with 56 m of ascent, it is the shortest and easiest of the four routes — Walking SA rates it Grade 2 Easy, and that assessment is fair. You can walk it in 30 minutes at a comfortable pace, or slow it down and take your time without pressure.

That said, “easy” in a reservoir reserve context still means formed gravel and dirt trails with a modest elevation variation between 146 m and 162 m. The surface is good throughout but includes sandy shore sections on the eastern and western edges where the path runs close to the water. This isn’t difficult walking, but it’s different enough from a park path to feel purposeful.

The purple trail markers are clearly placed throughout and the loop is simple to follow. A colour-coded trail board at the trailhead carpark shows all four Happy Valley routes — the Southern Loop is the most compact circuit on that board.

The Setting

Like the other Happy Valley walks, the Southern Loop is contained within the SA Water catchment reserve surrounding the reservoir. Native bushland flanks the path on the landward side, with water views opening up near the shore sections. The reservoir is a working water supply — no swimming, no fishing, no watercraft.

Birdlife is a constant companion. Wrens, honeyeaters and waterbirds are commonly encountered, and the quieter nature of a shorter loop means there’s less foot traffic to disturb them.

Who It’s For

The Southern Loop works well as:

  • A first walk for someone new to the reserve
  • A short outing when time or fitness doesn’t allow a longer circuit
  • A family walk with younger children
  • A warm-up before combining with the Woodland Loop on the same visit

The trailhead carpark has toilets, picnic shelters and BBQ facilities, which makes it an easy base for a longer outing across multiple loops.

Practical Notes

  • Purple trail markers — follow the colour-coded board at the carpark
  • Creek crossing included — check conditions after rain
  • Sandy footing on eastern and western shore sections
  • Reserve closes on Total Fire Ban days — check cfs.sa.gov.au
  • Gates locked at closing time — 5:00 pm in winter, 8:00 pm in summer
  • No dogs anywhere in the reserve
entry.summary: Happy Valley Reservoir Southern Loop: the easiest, shortest trail here — a 2.39 km easy loop ~20 km south of Adelaide, SA. Map & free GPX.

entry.title: Happy Valley Reservoir Woodland Loop — Trail Review

link.title: Happy Valley Reservoir Woodland Loop — Trail Review

entry.content:
The Walk

The Woodland Loop is the middle-ground option among Happy Valley Reservoir’s four walking tracks. At 3.87 km with 65 m of elevation gain, it covers more ground and terrain than the Southern Loop without pushing into the demanding territory of the Shoreline or Boundary circuits. It opened in December 2021 as part of the expanded trail network around the reservoir.

The walk follows yellow trail markers through native eucalypt woodland to the north of the reservoir. The woodland setting is notably different from the shoreline-adjacent sections of the other loops — you get more shade, more birdlife in the canopy, and less direct exposure to summer heat. The trade-off is fewer open water views.

There is one creek crossing approximately halfway through the circuit. In dry conditions it presents no difficulty. After heavy rainfall it can become uncrossable, at which point you’d need to backtrack. The trailhead noticeboard carries current condition updates — worth a look before you set off.

The Terrain

The elevation range sits between 150 m and 168 m, making this a genuinely undulating walk rather than a flat one. The climbs are short and the descents manageable, but the cumulative effect over 4 km means it’s a step up from a park path. Grade 3 Moderate is the correct classification.

The surface is consistently formed gravel and compacted dirt. Good walking shoes or trail runners are appropriate — waterproof footwear is worthwhile if there’s been recent rain.

The Trailhead

The Chandlers Hill Road / Kenihans Road roundabout carpark is the base for all four Happy Valley Reservoir walks. Facilities here include:

  • Flush toilets
  • Picnic shelters
  • BBQ
  • Drinking water fountain
  • Wheelchair-accessible facilities
  • Colour-coded trail map board

All four walks begin and end at this carpark, which makes it easy to combine loops or attempt different circuits on return visits.

Practical Notes

  • Check the creek crossing status before heading out — the trailhead noticeboard has current conditions
  • Yellow trail markers throughout — look for the trail board at the carpark junction
  • Reserve closes on Total Fire Ban days — check cfs.sa.gov.au
  • Gates locked at closing time — 5:00 pm in winter, 8:00 pm in summer
  • No dogs permitted anywhere in the reserve
  • No mountain bikes on this loop
entry.summary: Happy Valley Reservoir Woodland Loop: a short, easy 3.87 km bushland loop ~20 km south of Adelaide, SA. Family-friendly, map & free GPX.
